conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—the EPDS for short. It’s simply 10 questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, everything stays between us, and we can pause anytime. Ready to start?

**Question 1**  
Over the last week, have you still been able to enjoy things the way you used to, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

Honestly? Most things just feel kind of… flat. I used to love putting on a podcast and making a new recipe while I folded laundry, and now even that feels like another chore. When my partner tries to get me to watch our favorite show, I sit there but I’m not really laughing. Every once in a while I’ll get a flicker of “oh, this is nice,” but it fades fast. So, no—I’m not enjoying stuff the way I did before the baby came.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not very often. I’ll catch myself half-smiling if the baby does something cute, but real laughter feels rare. My partner will make a joke that normally would have me cracking up, and I just… can’t. It’s like the switch is stuck.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I mean, I try to tell myself, “It’ll be fun to take the baby for a walk tomorrow,” but the second I think about actually doing it, I just feel tired and kind of hopeless. Even little things—like a friend texting to come over for coffee—sound exhausting instead of exciting.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… more than I’d like to admit. Yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking it must be something I ate, or that I’m not soothing him right. When he spit up all over the clean outfit I just wrestled him into, the first thing in my head was, “Of course, I can’t even dress my own kid properly.” I know, rationally, babies cry and spit up, but I still land on “it’s my fault” almost every time.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most of the time, yeah. My mind just spins—like I’ll lie in bed listening to him breathe in the bassinet, and suddenly I’m sure he’s too hot, or too cold, or the swaddle’s too tight, or not tight enough. I’ll check on him three, four times, even when nothing’s wrong. I know the doctor said he’s perfectly healthy, but I can’t shake the feeling that something bad is about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes it hits me out of nowhere—my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get a full breath. The other night I was warming a bottle and suddenly pictured myself dropping it, glass shattering, scalding milk everywhere. I had to sit on the kitchen floor and count my breaths until the shaking stopped. There wasn’t any real danger, but in that moment it felt like something awful was seconds away.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… a lot of the time. I’ll look around at the dishes piled up, the laundry basket overflowing, the baby needing to be fed, and it feels like a tidal wave. I start one task, notice two others, and freeze. I tell myself, “Just finish the bottle, then move on,” but my chest gets tight and I end up crying over the sink because everything feels like too much. I usually get through the essentials, but it’s like I’m crawling to the finish line every day.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll finally get the baby down and crawl into bed myself, but then my brain just won’t shut off. I keep replaying every little thing I did that day—did I burp him long enough, did I snap at my partner, should I have sterilized the pacifier again. Some nights I watch the clock slide past two, three, four a.m., and when I do drift off I jolt awake at every tiny grunt from the bassinet. It’s like the sadness and the worries are talking over each other so loud I can’t settle.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most days, yeah. It’s like there’s this gray fog hanging over everything. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel tears sliding down my cheeks for no clear reason. I keep thinking I should be grateful—he’s here, he’s healthy—but I just feel hollow and weepy. Even when I try to “snap out of it,” the sadness sits heavy in my chest.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… sometimes it feels like the tears are sitting right behind my eyes waiting. I’ll be changing his diaper and suddenly I’m crying—quiet, steady tears I didn’t even see coming. It happened yesterday in the grocery store parking lot; I couldn’t find my keys and I just sat there sobbing. I feel silly afterward, but in the moment it’s like the sadness just spills out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel low, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. My baby needs me, and no matter how bad it gets I want to be here for him.

You've shared how the joy you once found in small pleasures-podcasts, cooking, laughing with your partner-has faded since your baby arrived. Most days feel flat, overshadowed by a gray fog of sadness, frequent tears, and a sense that even simple tasks are overwhelming. You describe constant worry about your baby's safety, sudden panic-like surges, and nights spent ruminating instead of sleeping, yet you remain firmly committed to caring for your little one. **Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include Patient reports markedly reduced laughter and humor, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now., Response conveys marked anhedonia and inability to anticipate pleasure, aligning with "Hardly at all", Patient acknowledges frequent, almost automatic self-blame ("almost every time") and provides a vivid recent example of unnecessary guilt, aligning with "Yes, most of the time.", Patient reports near-constant, intrusive worries about the baby that persist despite reassurance, matching "Yes, very often", Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes without real danger, matching "Yes, sometimes", “most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all.”, Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by persistent, intrusive worries and sadness, matching "Yes, most of the time", "Yes, most of the time", Patient describes frequent, unexpected crying episodes that occur in routine situations, matching "Yes, quite often") **Reasoning:** A score of 24 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major depressive disorder with peripartum onset. You endorse pervasive low mood, loss of interest or pleasure, undue guilt, impaired sleep, psychomotor slowing, and recurrent thoughts of inadequacy, meeting core DSM-5 criteria. Frequent, unexplained anxiety and panic symptoms suggest a co-occurring anxiety disorder. No self-harm ideation is reported, but functional impairment is pronounced. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice. **Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:** 1. Arrange urgent appointment with your obstetrician, primary care provider, or a perinatal mental health specialist to discuss diagnosis and treatment options 2. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy such as interpersonal therapy or cognitive-behavioural therapy tailored for postpartum mood disorders 3. Discuss benefits and risks of antidepressant medication (e.g., sertraline) compatible with breastfeeding, if indicated 4. Plan practical support: enlist family or friends for night shifts, housework, or meal preparation to improve sleep and reduce overwhelm 5. Practice 5-minute breathing or grounding exercises when panic sensations arise; keep the baby close and place your feet flat on the floor to anchor yourself 6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS and safety review within one week, sooner if symptoms worsen or self-harm thoughts emerge 7. Keep emergency numbers handy: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline or your local 24-hour mental health crisis line for immediate help if distress escalates 8. Maintain gentle structure: one small achievable activity daily (a short walk, shower, or 10 minutes of music) to rebuild a sense of mastery and pleasure Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today’s date]  Source: self-report  Clinician: [name]

Symptoms / Concerns endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia  
- Marked loss of enjoyment (even routine baby activities feel exhausting)  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame re parenting tasks  
- Chronic worry, intrusive “what-if” thoughts, nocturnal hypervigilance  
- Panic-equivalent episodes (HR racing, breathlessness, catastrophic imagery)  
- Feeling overwhelmed/drowning in daily tasks, frequent “freezing”  
- Initial insomnia and middle insomnia linked to rumination  
- Daily crying spells, “gray fog,” mood incongruent with circumstances  

Pattern  
Consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; functional impact moderate (household tasks “crawling to finish line,” social withdrawal).  

Safety  
Denies thoughts of self-harm or harm to infant (Q10).  No suicidal ideation reported at this time.

Risk factors  
- Primiparous status, sleep deprivation, high self-expectations  
- Absence of protective factors: limited described support, minimal pleasure reinforcement

Screening impression  
Meets threshold for further evaluation for Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset and co-occurring Anxiety Disorder.  Recommend formal diagnostic assessment, psychoeducation, support mobilization, and discussion of evidence-based treatment options (therapy, pharmacologic or both).  Continue to monitor safety at every contact.

Next step  
Schedule comprehensive follow-up within one week; provide crisis line numbers and emergency instructions before leaving.
